body:
What is ionising radiation?

Ionising radiation is radiation energetic enough to remove electrons from atoms or molecules and thereby create ions. It can alter chemical bonds and affect living cells. This ability explains both its useful applications and its potential biological hazards.

Not all radiation is ionising. Visible light and radio waves, for example, are forms of electromagnetic radiation that are generally non-ionising. Medical X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation.

Radiation and radioactivity are not identical

Radioactivity is the spontaneous transformation of an unstable atomic nucleus, accompanied by the emission of particles or electromagnetic radiation. A radioactive isotope is also called a radionuclide or radioisotope.

Radiation refers to the emitted energy or particles. Ionising radiation may come from radioactive decay or from machines such as X-ray generators and particle accelerators.

For example, a cobalt-60 source emits radiation through radioactive decay. A conventional diagnostic X-ray machine produces X-rays electrically when operated and does not require a radioactive isotope to generate the X-ray beam.

Main types of ionising radiation

TypeNatureImportant characteristic
AlphaHelium nucleus with 2 protons and 2 neutronsStrongly ionising but generally poorly penetrating
BetaFast electron or positronIntermediate penetration, depending on energy
GammaHigh-energy electromagnetic photonPenetrating radiation from nuclear processes
X-rayHigh-energy electromagnetic photonOften produced by machines through electron interactions
NeutronElectrically neutral nuclear particlePenetrating radiation that can activate some materials

Alpha particles lose energy rapidly in matter and are usually stopped by a sheet of paper or the outer dead layer of skin. This does not make alpha-emitting substances harmless: if such material enters the body through inhalation, ingestion or a wound, it may cause significant internal exposure.

Beta particles generally penetrate further than alpha particles. Plastic or other suitable low-density materials are often used to shield beta radiation. Gamma rays and X-rays generally require denser or thicker shielding, such as lead or concrete. Neutrons are commonly moderated using hydrogen-rich materials such as water or suitable shielding materials.

The effectiveness of shielding depends on the radiation's energy, intensity and the shielding material's thickness. No single thin barrier is equally effective against every type of radiation.

Radiation exposure, irradiation and contamination

Irradiation means exposing an object or person to radiation. Radioactive contamination means radioactive material is present somewhere it is not intended or desired, such as on a surface, in food or inside a person's body.

An object can receive radiation without becoming radioactive. For instance, a patient undergoing an ordinary X-ray examination is irradiated but does not become radioactive merely because the examination occurred. Similarly, food processed under approved irradiation conditions does not become radioactive as a result of that treatment.

Exposure is not the same as contamination. Radiation can reach an object from a source at a distance; radioactive contamination requires radioactive material to be present on or within the object.

Radioactive half-life

The physical half-life of a radionuclide is the time required for half of its original radioactive nuclei to decay. It is also the time required for its activity to fall to half the initial value through radioactive decay alone.

For example, after 1 half-life, approximately half the original activity remains. After 2 half-lives, approximately 1-quarter remains. The half-life is a characteristic of the radionuclide and does not depend on the starting quantity of radioactive material.

Half-life matters in medicine because a diagnostic radioisotope should remain useful long enough for examination while unnecessary radiation exposure should be limited.

Units used in radiation science

QuantitySI unitMeaning
Radioactive activityBecquerel, Bq1 nuclear decay per second
Absorbed doseGray, Gy1 joule of radiation energy absorbed per kilogram
Equivalent or effective doseSievert, SvRadiation dose expressed with biological weighting factors

The gray measures absorbed energy per unit mass. The sievert is used in radiation protection because different types of radiation and different tissues do not necessarily face the same biological risk for the same absorbed dose.

Prelims focus

  • Alpha radiation consists of helium nuclei; beta radiation consists of electrons or positrons.
  • Gamma rays and X-rays are electromagnetic radiation.
  • Becquerel measures activity, gray measures absorbed dose and sievert is used for biologically weighted dose.
  • A radioactive half-life reduces the remaining activity to 1-half.
  • After 2 half-lives, approximately 1-quarter of the original activity remains.
  • Trap: Irradiation does not automatically mean radioactive contamination.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom, section 4.6, printed pp. 52-53; International Atomic Energy Agency, Identification of Radioactive Sources and Devices, definitions of ionisation, ionising radiation, irradiation, gamma radiation and half-life; International Atomic Energy Agency, Radiation Protection and Safety of Radiation Sources: International Basic Safety Standards, definitions of dose quantities; consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
Why radiation is useful in medicine

Ionising radiation can pass through tissues, be detected by specialised instruments, or damage cells when delivered in a controlled manner. These properties make it useful for diagnosis, treatment and sterilisation of medical products.

The basic distinction is the purpose of exposure. Diagnostic procedures aim to obtain clinically useful information while limiting unnecessary radiation. Therapeutic procedures deliberately deliver radiation to a selected target to treat disease, particularly certain cancers.

Diagnostic imaging with radioactive tracers

In nuclear medicine, a patient receives a small, medically controlled quantity of a radioactive substance, usually as part of a radiopharmaceutical. The substance travels through the body according to its chemical and biological properties. A suitable detector records radiation emitted from the tracer and helps produce images of an organ or its function.

This differs from a conventional X-ray image. In ordinary X-ray radiography, an external machine directs X-rays through the body and a detector measures the transmitted radiation. In nuclear medicine, the radiation used to form the image originates from the administered tracer.

Technetium-99m

Technetium-99m is widely used in diagnostic nuclear medicine. It emits gamma radiation that suitable cameras can detect. Different technetium-99m compounds can help examine the skeleton, heart, kidneys and other organs.

Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) uses detected gamma photons to reconstruct information about the distribution of a radiotracer. Technetium-99m is an important isotope associated with SPECT imaging.

Fluorine-18

Fluorine-18 is widely used in Positron Emission Tomography (PET), including in fluorine-18-labelled fluorodeoxyglucose imaging. Fluorine-18 emits positrons. When a positron encounters an electron, annihilation produces photons that PET scanners detect.

SPECT and PET are both nuclear medicine techniques, but their underlying radioactive emissions and detection methods differ.

Radiation therapy for cancer and thyroid disease

Radiotherapy uses ionising radiation to damage the genetic material of selected cells. Cancer cells may then lose their ability to reproduce. Healthy tissues can also be affected, which is why medical treatment requires carefully planned targeting and exposure.

External beam radiotherapy

In external beam radiotherapy, radiation is directed at a target inside the patient from equipment outside the body. Cobalt-60 has been used as a gamma-ray source in external radiotherapy. Modern radiotherapy may also use electrically powered linear accelerators that generate high-energy radiation without relying on a radioactive source in the treatment head.

Brachytherapy

Brachytherapy places a radiation source inside or very close to the area requiring treatment. Iridium-192 is an example of a radioisotope used in brachytherapy.

Radioiodine treatment

Iodine-131 is used for selected thyroid disorders, including treatment of an overactive thyroid and certain thyroid cancers. The thyroid naturally takes up iodine to produce thyroid hormones. This property allows administered radioactive iodine to concentrate in thyroid tissue.

Radioiodine therapy must not be described as the treatment for every thyroid swelling or every form of goitre. Its suitability depends on the diagnosis and clinical circumstances.

Important medical radioisotopes

RadioisotopePrincipal applicationImportant distinction
Technetium-99mDiagnostic nuclear imagingCommonly associated with gamma-camera and SPECT studies
Fluorine-18PET imagingPositron-emitting isotope
Iodine-131Selected thyroid treatmentsTherapeutic radioiodine
Cobalt-60Gamma-ray radiotherapyExternal radiation source
Iridium-192BrachytherapySource placed close to treatment region

Sterilisation of medical products

Radiation can destroy or inactivate microorganisms on medical products. Controlled gamma irradiation is used to sterilise suitable disposable healthcare products, such as certain syringes, dressings and other packaged devices.

One advantage is that suitable products can be sterilised after packaging, helping prevent subsequent microbial contamination. The irradiated product does not become radioactive merely because it was sterilised using an approved gamma-irradiation process.

Why medical radiation must be carefully controlled

Radiation can benefit patients, but unnecessary exposure can damage normal tissues and increase health risks. The medical use of radiation therefore requires clinical justification, suitable equipment, accurate treatment or imaging procedures, and appropriate protection of patients and workers.

Prelims focus

  • Technetium-99m is an important diagnostic radioisotope.
  • Fluorine-18 is associated with PET imaging.
  • Iodine-131 is used in selected thyroid treatments.
  • Cobalt-60 has been used in external gamma radiotherapy.
  • Iridium-192 is associated with brachytherapy.
  • Trap: Conventional X-ray imaging generally uses machine-generated radiation; nuclear medicine imaging uses administered radiotracers.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom, section 4.6, Applications, printed p. 53; International Atomic Energy Agency, Applications of Research Reactors, Nuclear Energy Series No. NP-T-5.3, 2014, Annex II, printed p. 92; International Atomic Energy Agency, Nuclear Medicine for Diagnosis and Treatment; Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Radiation Applications, medical and radiation-processing categories; consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
How radiation contributes to agriculture

Radiation and isotopic techniques can help improve crops, manage insect pests, study the movement of nutrients and preserve harvested food. These are different applications with different scientific purposes.

The central distinction is that some techniques use radiation to cause a biological change, while others use radioisotopes to trace the movement of a substance. Food irradiation uses controlled exposure to influence microorganisms, insects or biological processes in food.

Mutation breeding in crop improvement

Mutation breeding uses physical or chemical agents to increase genetic variation in plants. When radiation is the agent, seeds or other suitable plant material may be exposed to controlled gamma rays, X-rays or other ionising radiation.

Radiation can alter DNA and create mutations. Most changes are neutral or undesirable, but some may provide useful characteristics. Plant breeders grow and examine the treated material, identify potentially useful variants, and test whether their desirable characteristics remain stable in later generations.

Possible objectives include improved disease resistance, suitable maturity periods, plant size or other useful crop characteristics.

Mutation breeding is not the same as directly inserting a selected foreign gene. Radiation-induced mutations create variation, while breeding and selection determine whether any resulting plant is useful.

The radiation does not directly guarantee a better crop. The desired result depends on selecting and evaluating suitable plants after treatment.

Sterile Insect Technique

The Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) is a pest-management method in which large numbers of male insects are made infertile, often through controlled irradiation, and released into a target area.

When these sterile males mate with wild females, viable offspring are not produced from those matings. Repeated releases can gradually suppress the targeted insect population, provided the method is suitable for the species and local conditions.

SIT has been applied against several agricultural insect pests and is also being developed or tested for certain disease-transmitting mosquitoes.

The irradiated insects do not become radioactive as a consequence of the approved sterilisation process. SIT based on irradiation also does not require genetic modification of the insects.

Radioisotopes as agricultural tracers

A tracer is a detectable substance used to follow the movement or distribution of another substance within a system.

Radioisotopes can act as tracers because their radiation can be detected in very small quantities. For example, radioactive phosphorus-32 can be used in research to study the movement and uptake of phosphorus in soil-plant systems.

Such experiments help researchers understand nutrient availability and fertiliser-use efficiency. The radioactive material is used in a controlled investigation; its purpose is to provide information, not to increase a crop's productivity merely by exposing it to radiation.

What is food irradiation?

Food irradiation is the controlled exposure of food to specified forms of ionising radiation to achieve an intended preservation or safety effect.

Commonly used radiation sources include:

  • Gamma rays: produced from suitable radioactive sources, particularly cobalt-60.
  • Electron beams: produced using electrically powered accelerators.
  • X-rays: produced using suitable machines.

Radiation deposits energy in the food and in any organisms present. This energy can damage biological structures and disrupt processes needed for microorganisms to multiply, insects to develop or plant tissues to sprout.

Important food preservation applications

ApplicationIntended effectExamples
Sprout inhibitionReduces unwanted sprouting during storagePotatoes and onions
Microbial reductionReduces selected spoilage or disease-causing microorganismsSpices and suitable packaged foods
Insect disinfestationKills pests or prevents their further developmentGrains, cereals and pulses
Ripening or spoilage delayMay extend useful storage lifeSelected fruits and vegetables

Does irradiated food become radioactive?

Food treated under approved irradiation conditions does not become radioactive. The radiation transfers energy to the food, but this does not mean radioactive material is added to it.

Food irradiation also does not involve exposing food to a nuclear reactor's fuel or waste. An authorised facility controls the source, the exposure conditions and the treatment process.

Food irradiation is different from ordinary heating because it can achieve certain preservation effects without a large rise in food temperature. It is sometimes described as a cold process. However, the treatment must be appropriate for the food and its intended purpose.

It does not make spoiled food fresh again, eliminate every possible hazard, or remove the need for hygienic production, proper packaging and suitable storage.

Indian institutions and oversight

The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) has developed and promoted radiation-processing applications involving food, agricultural products, healthcare supplies and other materials.

In India, food irradiation facilities operate under applicable regulatory and food-safety requirements. These include the roles of the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) and relevant food-safety authorities, including the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI).

Prelims focus

  • Mutation breeding uses radiation to create genetic variation followed by selection.
  • SIT suppresses selected insect populations through the release of sterile males.
  • Phosphorus-32 is a radioactive tracer used in soil-plant nutrient studies.
  • Food irradiation can inhibit sprouting in potatoes and onions.
  • Cobalt-60 gamma rays, electron beams and X-rays can be used for authorised food irradiation.
  • Trap: Properly irradiated food does not become radioactive, and irradiation does not replace food hygiene.

[Sources: Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Food Irradiation, sections How Irradiation Works and Food Applications; Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Setting Up of a Gamma Radiation Processing Plant, applications and regulatory requirements; International Atomic Energy Agency, Sterile Insect Technique for Mosquitoes, Frequently Asked Questions; Joint FAO/IAEA Division, Mutation Induction in Plants by Ionizing Radiation, 1985, programme description; International Atomic Energy Agency, Phosphorus Isotopes in Agricultural Studies, technical guidance on tracer applications; consulted 16 November 2026.]
